newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac in call to hustings, stages unity display.
newsitem.headline: Chirac in call to hustings, stages unity display.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac gave his centre-right ministers their election campaign orders on Wednesday and staged a show of reconciliation with a former presidential rival, fellow Gaullist Edouard Balladur.
The first opinion poll taken since Chirac called a snap election for May 25 and June 1 suggested the ruling coalition would win comfortably but with a sharply reduced majority.
The European Commission meanwhile gave the government a boost by forecasting that France would meet the key budget deficit criterion for entry into a single European currency.
Chirac told ministers at a weekly cabinet meeting: "You must continue to govern and fulfil your duties to the full but you are also political leaders.

"You must contribute to feeding the political debate by going out to meet the French people and conveying to them your convictions, your energy, your confidence and your enthusiasm," government spokesman Alain Lamassoure quoted him as saying.

In a timely unity gesture, Chirac invited former prime minister Balladur for only their second private meeting since they clashed bitterly for the presidency in 1995. It lasted 45 minutes and neither man commented afterwards, although both smiled as they shook hands.
When Balladur called on Chirac last July, photographers were barred from the Elysee presidential palace courtyard and only managed to shoot grainy pictures through the gates.

The ex-premier, who has stayed away from most coalition and Gaullist party gatherings since Chirac defeated him for the presidency, was given pride of place on the platform on Tuesday when Prime Minister Alain Juppe outlined his campaign agenda.
Chief Balladur lieutenant Nicolas Sarkozy, also rehabilitated as one of the coalition's spokesmen, ruled out any further austerity measures should the centre-right win.

Asked about opinion poll findings that most voters expect tougher austerity should the bloc win, Sarkozy told RTL radio: "There will not be tougher austerity, and no increase in taxes...Of all developed countries, we are the ones with the heaviest burden of taxes."

The opposition Socialists, who have accused Chirac of preparing a harsh new round of austerity to help meet criteria for joining a planned European single currency, reasserted conditions for membership.

The party also said that creation of a single currency from 1999 was a political decison that should not be clouded by dogmatic economic criteria. It said that neither France nor Germany would comply with all criteria.
"We want the single currency, but with conditions," party spokesman Francois Hollande said.

The Socialists want Italy and Spain to be in from the start -- Britain too if it wants. They also want the creation of a European political authority to counterbalance the power of a central bank and the creation of an EU jobs pact, and they demand the euro not be overvalued against the dollar.

But the European Commission said on Wednesday that France was on course to meet the toughest test for monetary union by holding its public deficit to 3.0 percent of gross domestic product this year and next.

Financial markets were calmer after three days of jitters caused by uncertainty generated by the early election. The franc, fixed income and stock markets were stronger partly on the poll showing the centre-right would win.
A CSA poll forecast that the centre-right would win 332 of the 555 seats in metropolitan France to 222 for the combined left-wing opposition and one for the far-right National Front.
The coalition held 464 of the 577 seats in the outgoing assembly, including most of the 22 seats in overseas departments and territories which are not covered by opinion polls.
